coding_context.description: Input, Process, and Output Anxiety Scales predict general language learning anxiety
coding_context.reported_success_quote:
In both the initial as well as the replication study, evidence showed
that language learners experience significantly higher levels of output anxiety than
input or process anxiety; nonetheless, these three types of anxiety were found to be
linked to the general concept of language anxiety to different degrees, with process
anxiety depicting the strongest association according to the results of data analysis
in the initial and the replication study.
Although the scales could be characterized as reliable, their componential struc-
ture was found to be not without flaws. Some of the same items of the scales were
labelled as problematic in the Hungarian version of the scales as well as in the English
version. As such, it can be said that these issues are inherent to the items rather than
to their translated versions and thus warrant reconsideration.

coding_context.description: In this paper, the authors offer insight into a previously documented observation known as the left-digit bias, whereby consumers tend to give greater weight to the left-most digit when comparing two prices. This means, for example, that consumers tend to treat a price difference of $4.00 vs. $2.99 as larger than $4.01 vs. $3.00. The authors’ key claim is that this bias is greater when the prices are presented side-by-side, in a way that makes them easier to compare, than sequentially, on two separate but consecutive screens.
coding_context.reported_success_quote: We find marginally significant support for the authors’ key interaction in both replications. [...] Although the evidence is much weaker than in the original study, we are inclined to believe that the original effect is real.

coding_context.reported_success_quote:
Newly collected data corroborated Irwin et al.’s (2013) finding that encouragement using the
ambiguous and exclusive pronoun “you” (e.g. “you can do it”) from a virtually present partner
significantly weakened this Köhler effect. Some partial support was found for Irwin et al.’s expla-
nation of this effect. Irwin et al. suggested that when one hears one’s partner say things like “you
can do it!”, that may be interpreted that the partner is him/herself struggling and is to some degree
trying to encourage him/herself. Hence, that partner may not be as superior as previously thought.

coding_context.reported_success_quote:
Newly collected data corroborated Irwin et al.’s (2013) finding that encouragement using the
ambiguous and exclusive pronoun “you” (e.g. “you can do it”) from a virtually present partner
significantly weakened this Köhler effect. Some partial support was found for Irwin et al.’s expla-
nation of this effect. Irwin et al. suggested that when one hears one’s partner say things like “you
can do it!”, that may be interpreted that the partner is him/herself struggling and is to some degree
trying to encourage him/herself. Hence, that partner may not be as superior as previously thought.

items.worker_notes: Only assigned unfinished fields are completed. All other fields are placeholders. The narrative verdict is coded mixed because the authors explicitly describe greater prime responsiveness for high but not low self-conscious participants; this is a conditional author conclusion, not a verdict inferred from p values. The combined-analysis statement that the prime effect replicates Bargh et al. is not treated as a separate-study unconditional verdict. Target-match identifies the study/outcome supporting assigned fields only, not any unassigned statistic.

However, as we did
not replicate the original effects in a first experiment, in spite of the fact that our materials and our
procedure resembled the original study as closely as possible, we conducted a second experiment with
an even stronger accountability manipulation as compared to the original study, and with an increased
sample size. Once again, no effects of accountability were found. Taken together, the results of these two
experiments question the robustness of the original findings.

coding_context.description: Participants who encounter scarcity salience in a prior unrelated context would be more likely to use the provided products in novel but appropriate ways to solve the given task (differences between the scarcity condition and the abundance condition)
coding_context.reported_success_quote:
A chi-square test revealed no significant effect of resource availability on the correctness
of the solutions (X2 (2, N = 319) = 2.224, p = .329). We next conducted a binary logistic
regression analysis to assess the differences between the conditions. The results showed
that there were no significant differences between the scarcity condition (M=27%) and
the abundance condition (M = 29%, B = -.02, [SE] = .06, Wald = .063, p = .802), and
that there was no significant difference between the scarcity condition and the control
condition (M = 36%, B = -.09, [SE] = .06, Wald = 1.90, p = .174.) Furthermore, we
observed no difference between the abundance and control conditions (B = -.07, [SE] =
.06, Wald = 1.2, p = .278). Including careless responders did not qualitatively change
the key study result: there was still no significant difference between the scarcity and
control condition (M = 36%, B = -.10, [SE] = .06, Wald = 2.422, p = .120).

items.worker_notes: Both assigned rows have identical neutral descriptions, p.4 locators, and study identifiers. No outcome or contrast distinguishes them. No row-order or numeric matching used. The replication is general Chinese adults aged 18–75 (Table 1), rather than the original young adults aged 17–24 in the description. Candidate critical tests on p.4 section 3.5: typical eating disorder symptomatology omnibus chi-square 47.78, p < .001; muscularity-oriented eating disorder symptomatology omnibus chi-square 50.40, p < .001; psychosocial impairment omnibus chi-square 115.88, p < .001; emotion regulation difficulties omnibus chi-square 128.12, p < .001. Typical symptomatology pairwise candidates: EOE versus EOE-EUE chi-square 8.29, p = .004, d = .39; EOE versus EUE chi-square 27.02, p < .001, d = .69; EOE versus non-EE chi-square 40.98, p < .001, d = .92. Muscularity symptomatology pairwise candidates: EOE versus non-EE chi-square 30.87, p < .001, d = .84; EOE versus EUE chi-square 31.79, p < .001, d = .81; EOE-EUE versus non-EE chi-square 18.41, p < .001, d = .56; EOE-EUE versus EUE chi-square 18.81, p < .001, d = .51; EOE versus EOE-EUE chi-square 3.58, p = .058, d = .27. There are additional pairwise psychosocial impairment and emotion regulation tests on pp.4–5, sex-membership odds ratios in section 3.4, and LCA fit comparisons in Table 2. None is uniquely assigned by these locators. Candidate common sample only: Table 1 n = 600 and section 2.1 final 600 adults after 33 validity-test exclusions. items.worker_notes:
Identity verified from supplied text: matching title Can failure be made productive also in Bayesian reasoning? A conceptual replication study, Katharina Loibl and Timo Leuders, DOI 10.1007/s11251-024-09670-y, ORIGINAL RESEARCH, online 12 July 2024, final issue Instructional Science (2025) 53:1739–1758. Primary replication research report with full methods, results, discussion and references. No PDF supplied. Original side and unassigned fields are placeholders only. Target ambiguous: the neutral description combines attempted problem solving, awareness and conceptual understanding, without naming a unique measured test. Separate candidates are conceptual-learning order-of-phases ANOVA (hypothesis 1a), its rank-transformed sensitivity analysis, exploratory solution-attempt frequencies and discussion-level awareness explanation. No target inferred from repeated descriptions, row order or numeric matching. Candidate conceptual ANOVA: F(1,71) = 0.12, p = .73, partial eta squared = 0.002; sensitivity F(1,71) = 0.06, p = .81, partial eta squared = 0.001. Candidate conceptual-model N = 75 (Table 7); exploratory PS-first subgroup N = 38. Neither N is assigned to unresolved target. Evidence: One ANOVA with the dependent variable conceptual
knowledge outcome tested hypothesis 1a (main effect of order of phases), hypothesis 2
(main effect of type of instruction), and hypothesis 3 (interaction). | Out of the 38 students, 31 students generated only one solution attempt, 6 students gen-
erated two solution attempts, and 1 student generated three solution attempts. | One reason for the students’ limited problem-
solving processes may be that students did not become aware of their knowledge gaps.

This is a full primary brief report (abstract, methods, results, discussion, references), not an abstract-only parse. No PDF is assigned. The Supplement is referenced but is not contained in the supplied source. Description specifies reaction time but no ANOVA term. TASK, EMOTION, TASK × EMOTION and collectively reported GROUP effects are distinct candidates; p. 4 does not uniquely identify one. RT candidate tests: TASK F1,72=405.55, p<0.001, partial eta-squared=0.849; EMOTION F3.53,254.18=131.98, p<0.001, partial eta-squared=0.647; TASK × EMOTION F3.20,230.38=105.87, p<0.001, partial eta-squared=0.595; all GROUP main/interaction effects are reported only collectively as Fs<1, without exact Fs, p values or partial eta-squared. No test selected from these candidates. Candidate common main-report analytic sample: 33 AN + 41 HC = 74 adolescent participants in mutually exclusive included groups; not derived from degrees of freedom. Main report describes the mixed TASK × EMOTION × GROUP ANOVAs and no additional participant exclusions for those reported models. Eligibility excludes IQ <85, visual impairments, specified neurological/psychiatric disorders and substance abuse; HC excludes current/past mental disorders. Endnote 2 describes a separate sensitivity analysis excluding two AN participants above the 10th BMI percentile; this is not substituted for the main analysis. Model sample cannot be assigned to an unidentified row-specific test; retain only as a candidate. Misclassification model inclusion/exclusions cannot be verified without Supplement. Authors explicitly describe successful replication at whole-study level; reported_success preserves that narrative verdict only, not a claim of a uniquely identified row-specific test. No mapping is inferred from row order, original statistics or numeric agreement.

GROUP and EMOTION × GROUP collectively Fs≤1.50, ps>0.1. Emotion-task follow-ups: EMOTION F3.33,239.86=72.19, p<0.001, partial eta-squared=0.501; GROUP F1,72=4.59, p=0.036, partial eta-squared=0.060; EMOTION × GROUP F3.33,239.86=2.79, p=0.036, partial eta-squared=0.037. coding_context.description: Scarcity leads to over-borrowing.
coding_context.reported_success_quote:
In the subsequent replications, we find consistent and strong evidence for the motivating
hypothesis of the original paper: Scarcity itself leads to over-borrowing. We see this clearly in
Experiments 2, 3, and 4 where poor participants performed significantly worse when they had
the flexibility to borrow. [...] But we did not find a greater focus on the current round (estimated via
the amount of time spent aiming shots) to be associated with higher borrowing rates.

coding_context.reported_success_quote:
Our results largely confirm the evidence documented in Poole for Brazil which suggests that when workers
leave multinationals and are rehired at domestic establishments, the wages of their new coworkers
who have already been present in the establishment increase. However, unlike suggested in the
original article there is little indication that these spillovers differ in a statistically significant way
across various dimensions of heterogeneity for any of the three countries.

Header has provisional volume/issue/pagination (Vol. 111, No. 9, 000), unlike the final bibliographic issue, but title/authors/DOI identify the work. No PDF was supplied. Original source and unassigned fields were not examined; their schema entries are placeholders. The broad description and page-6 F locator leave two reading comparisons, ART main effects and interactions possible. Original study identifiers do not uniquely identify a pooled replication term. Candidate evidence (not assigned values): p. 6 literary versus popular condition: 25.99), F(1, 191) ⫽ 0.83, p ⫽ .363, d ⫽ 0.05.; ART predictor: F(1, 288) = 95.16, p < .001, b = 0.37; ART × condition F(1, 288) = 0.67, p = .412. Literary versus no-reading condition: for those who had read nothing (Madj. ⫽ 26.25), F(1, 53.6) ⫽ 0.08, ... p ⫽ .775, d ⫽ 0.01.; ART predictor F(1, 361) = 139.37, p < .001; interaction F(1, 361) = 4.06, p = .045, with conditional b = 0.37 (no reading) and b = 0.26 (literary). Comparison N candidates printed p. 4: popular 303; no reading 369. These are candidate model Ns only, not assigned analytic Ns. Page 6 footnote 3 explicitly identifies the conditional b values as unstandardized coefficients in a model with transformed ART/RMET. No conversion performed. Reported_success refers to the authors’ paper-level verdict on immediate reading effects, not to the significant lifetime ART association.

input.description: Article. The annotation covers OCs of (in)definite articles (a(n)/the). Given that the ‘zero article’ was disregarded in previous MOS, it was also disregarded here for comparative purposes. The non-suppliance of an article in an (in)definite OC was tagged as omission. Also, given that both definite and indefinite articles were analysed as a single morpheme in previous MOS, we analysed them similarly, even if we are aware that they are better analysed separately as they do not emerge simultaneously (cf. the discussion in Section 4.4). Selection of one article for the other was tagged as ‘mis-selection’. The forms a/an were understood as spelling variants, so selection of one when the other was expected was not tagged as NTLU. Importantly, determining the OC of the/a(n) is based on information-status distinctions deriving from discourse, i.e., on whether the entity has been previously mentioned in the discourse (i.e., discourse-old, topic) or not (i.e., discourse-new, focus), and therefore whether or not the referent is known to the reader. Articles were annotated independently of the appearance of characters in the picture story, which could give the sense of old information, but technically introduce discoursenew information when retelling the story to a reader. Therefore, ILA considers hearer/reader knowledge (and not speaker knowledge) to determine discourse-old/discourse-new distinctions (cf. Hawkins, 2001).

coding_context.reported_success_quote: we replicated earlier findings that prosociality was associated with a greater level of secure attachment and a lower level of avoidant attachment. Moreover, prosociality was positively related to the number of siblings, especially sisters, as discovered by Study 3 of the original study. However, we failed to replicate the significant relation between SVO and age. Generally, we conclude that prosocial orientation is associated—even if modestly—with secure and avoidant attachment and the number of siblings, but the link with age is a question open to future investigation.

coding_context.description: Hand-washing after experiencing disgust led participants to judge moral vignettes with less severity than participants who did not wash their hands
coding_context.reported_success_quote:
We did not find evidence that physical cleanliness reduced the severity of moral judgments using samples sizes that provided over .99
power to detect the original effect sizes. Our estimates of the overall effect size were much smaller than estimates from Experiment 1 (original
d = 0.60, 95% CI [1.23, 0.04], N = 40; replication d = 0.01, 95% CI [0.28, 0.26], N = 208) and Experiment 2 (original d = 0.85, 95%
CI [1.47, 0.22], N = 43; replication d = 0.01, 95% CI [.34, 0.36], N = 126). These findings suggest that the population effect sizes are
probably substantially smaller than the original estimates.

This is the primary replication report with methods, results, Tables 1–3, conclusions and references, not an abstract or secondary excerpt. No PDF was supplied. All five replication locators are p. 4 with blank description and study identifiers. No row-specific target correspondence is established. Page 4 includes female giving-versus-taking (p-value = 0.93), gender within giving (p-value = 0.70), gender within taking (p-value = 0.67), total OLS gender/framing terms, interactions, sex-specific OLS and logistic analyses. Table 1 (p. 3) prints replication Mann-Whitney p = 0.924 (all giving versus taking), 0.725 (male), 0.927 (female), 0.699 (male versus female giving), 0.665 (male versus female taking). Table 2 (p. 5) prints OLS coefficients Giving Game 0.319 and Female 0.259 in first total model; TG*Female 0.497, GG*Male 0.539, GG*Female 0.559 in second total model; Giving Game 0.483 male and 0.071 female. These are printed amount-allocation coefficients, not printed Cohen d; no conversion performed. Table 2 explicit observations are 137 in each total model, 74 male, 63 female. These model Ns remain candidates only because the target is unresolved. Table 1 has 69/68 total, 37/37 male, 32/31 female observations per treatment. No N sum or df derivation performed. Recruitment 274 includes 137 dictators and 137 recipients, and is not substituted for analytic N. No target-specific exclusions established. Table 3 (p. 6) reports distinct logistic analyses of allocating nothing with total/male/female samples. Paper-wide verdict mixed is not a row-specific verdict.

coding_context.reported_success_quote:
Newly collected data corroborated Irwin et al.’s (2013) finding that encouragement using the
ambiguous and exclusive pronoun “you” (e.g. “you can do it”) from a virtually present partner
significantly weakened this Köhler effect. Some partial support was found for Irwin et al.’s expla-
nation of this effect. Irwin et al. suggested that when one hears one’s partner say things like “you
can do it!”, that may be interpreted that the partner is him/herself struggling and is to some degree
trying to encourage him/herself. Hence, that partner may not be as superior as previously thought.

Full published primary research report, including both experiments, analyses, tables, discussion and references; not an abstract or secondary article. No PDF was supplied. Assigned study_r 2 suggests Experiment 2. Description does not distinguish accuracy from RT, current- versus previous-trial demand, main effects versus follow-up comparisons. No row-order or numerical matching used. Experiment 2 previous-load main-effect candidates: accuracy F(1, 6530) = 15.37, p < .001 (printed p.25, PDF page 10); RT F(1, 6530) = 24.64, p = .027 AS PRINTED (printed p.26, PDF page 11). RT follow-up beta = –36.11 has p < .001 and dz = 0.21; this is a different test and its p must not replace the main-effect p. Other candidate mnemonic-load main effects: current-load accuracy F(1,6530) = 111.33, p < .001; current-load RT F(1,6530) = 434.25, p < .001. Table 4 prints log-odds/RT parameter estimates; no conversion performed. Common Experiment 2 model candidate Nobs = 6,612 trial observations nested within 76 retained participants; 100 recruited, 24 excluded for diagnoses/psychotropic medications, no RT outlier trials, remaining participants responded to more than one third of trials. Counts explicit, not inferred from df or summed. As the row-specific test is unresolved, model N is only a candidate for parent field-scope review. Authors explicitly describe replication of the mnemonic-demand result over two experiments (p.29); reported_success is that broad narrative verdict, not a verdict on every interaction/contrast. Locator p.7 (printed p.22) contains Experiment 1 accuracy Table 2 and previous-trial accuracy analyses, not Experiment 2. Candidate previous-load accuracy F(1, 6702) = 24.26, p < .001; previous load by interference F(1, 6702) = 4.99, p = .026; multiple OR follow-ups also occur. No unique Experiment 2 target established.

coding_context.description: The current study investigated whether mnemonic demands, in a working memory (WM) task, can drive similar online control modifications.
coding_context.reported_success_quote: Consistent with Jha and Kiyonaga, the present results revealed that mnemonic load led to dynamic adjustments in cognitive control, as reflected by greater performance on trials preceded by high than by low load. In addition, we observed that affective interference could trigger dynamic adjustments in cognitive control, as evinced by higher performance on trials preceded by negative than by neutral distractors.

coding_context.description: Whether holding decision makers accountable for the decision process decreases escalating commitment, while accountability for the decision outcomes increases it.
coding_context.reported_success_quote:
However, as we did
not replicate the original effects in a first experiment, in spite of the fact that our materials and our
procedure resembled the original study as closely as possible, we conducted a second experiment with
an even stronger accountability manipulation as compared to the original study, and with an increased

duplicate all procedural and methodological details of the original study (i.e., same cover story, experimental manipula-
